SM17A-A2.free_elimination: none found. Options -21, 6, 11, 59 are all integers, all reachable as c from a linear equation of the same shape, and no sign, parity or magnitude argument separates them: the max is c and f(1)=c-8, so c=2c-11 has a unique solution with no bound on its sign. -21 is the only negative but the condition does not force c>0 without solving. No printed-number echo (stem prints 2,3,1,5; 6=2*3 is the only echo and it is a distractor, which is the right direction).
SM17A-A2.note: Clean. All three distractors are named misreads with working solve programs, and each perturbs a DIFFERENT mechanism (sign of the squared term, scope of 'twice', sign of the vertex shift). No wrong method found that lands on 11: the two natural misreads give 6 and -21, and reading the max as f(1) gives 3, off-list. Labelled hard; it is one substitution plus one linear equation, which is medium on the module-2 hard route.

SM17A-A3.free_elimination: none found. Closure check: 15 is not the arithmetic mean of 8 and 18 (13), 8 and 18 are not in geometric relation to 15, and 48 is unrelated. Parity gives nothing (8,18,48 even, 15 odd, and a+b has no forced parity). Printed-number echo is weak and points at distractors (15=a*b, 48=45+3), not at the key.
SM17A-A3.note: Correct and clean but very easy: 1215/45=27 is the friendliest possible cube, and both a and b come out single-digit. The '15 is the product not the sum' distractor is the strongest one. No wrong method reaches 8. Labelled medium; on the hard route this is easy and should not be drawn into module 2.

SM17A-A4.free_elimination: THREE STRUCK, and this is the item's defect. The answer form (3x + a)/(x - b) spends the printed 3, leaving exactly two unused printed constants, 5 and 12. Of the four options, 15 = 3*5 and 36 = 3*12 reuse the already-spent 3, and 17 = 5 + 12 is a sum where the stem asks for a product ab. Only 60 = 5*12 is the product of the two LEFTOVER printed numbers. The elimination survives the ambiguity that would otherwise sink it: whether a=12,b=5 or a=5,b=12, the product is 60 either way, so the guesser does not even have to decide which is which. No inversion, no algebra, no arithmetic beyond recognising three products and one sum.
SM17A-A4.note: DROP. The key is recoverable from the printed-number bookkeeping alone. The intended work (clear the fraction, collect x, factor) is entirely bypassed by 'multiply the two constants the answer form did not already use'. Asking for ab rather than, say, a - b or a + 2b is what creates the symmetry that makes the shortcut immune to getting a and b backwards. Not repairable by swapping distractors: any option set built from the same three printed constants regenerates the tell. Re-author with a different queried combination and at least one option that is also a leftover-pair product.

SM17A-A5.free_elimination: none found. Simplified stem: the denominator 6x^2-x-12 is already (2x-3)(3x+4), so no cancellation shortcut exists. Sign: both a and b come out positive but nothing in the option set is negative, so that strikes nothing. Closure: 29, 40, 45, 53 are not related by mean of any kind (arith mean of 29 and 53 is 41, not offered; 40 and 45 are not means of any pair). Parity: 29, 45, 53 odd and 40 even, but a+b has no forced parity. Printed-number echo: 40 IS the correct b, which is a trap rather than an elimination.
SM17A-A5.note: Strong item. The explanation's claim is true and is the item's best property: a = 7*3 - 4*2 and b = 7*4 + 4*3, so neither constant can be read off without performing the whole expansion, and the partial-credit distractor 40 punishes stopping at b. No wrong method lands on 53 -- the sign slip gives 29, the add-instead-of-subtract gives 45. The shortcut a+b = N(1) = 7(7) - 4(-1) = 53 is a legitimate evaluation, not a leak.

SM17A-A6.free_elimination: none found, and the set is well built against residue attack. Substituting x=1 gives p(1) = 3*Q(1) + R(1) = 7, so m+n+p+q = 1 - 2(m+n), which is odd -- and ALL FOUR options (-1, 5, 9, 17) are odd, so the parity channel is closed deliberately. No option is a printed coefficient of the dividend or divisor. No monotonicity or bound argument applies to a sum of four signed constants.
SM17A-A6.note: WRONG METHOD LANDS ON THE KEY -- flag. The natural cheap route is to substitute x=1: p(1) = 2-3+5+7-4 = 7, and a solver who forgets that the divisor evaluates to 1+2 = 3 (not 1) writes Q(1)+R(1) = 7, then subtracts the quotient's known leading 2 to get m+n+p+q = 5. That is the key. It works only because Q(1) = 2-3+1 = 0 makes 3*Q(1)+R(1) and Q(1)+R(1) coincide. The method is genuinely invalid -- the correct identity leaves two unknowns and cannot solve the item at all -- so a solver who uses it is rewarded for an error. Fixable without touching the option set: perturb the dividend so the quotient does not sum to zero at x=1. Otherwise the best item in the batch for length and error surface, and correctly labelled hard.

SM17A-A7.free_elimination: ONE STRUCK, by parity, and it is not the one the explanation names. Both points lie on y = 2x+4, so y1+y2 = 2(x1+x2) + 8; x1+x2 is minus the x-coefficient of the difference quadratic, a difference of two printed integers, hence an integer, so y1+y2 must be EVEN. That kills -1 outright, with no arithmetic beyond noticing that the coefficient of x is integral. Options -14, 6, 10 survive. The explanation instead nominates -14 as 'the one strikeable option' because it is the bare difference -10-4 of two printed constants; that strike is softer than the parity one and points at a different option, so the batch's self-audit has located the wrong single strike. Combined they would leave 6 and 10, but the second strike is a heuristic about authoring habits rather than a mathematical constraint, so I score the item at one.
SM17A-A7.note: Keep. One free strike is inside tolerance and the surviving pair 6 / 10 differ only by the sign slip the item is built to catch. The irrational roots (-1 +/- sqrt(57))/2 genuinely block backsolving, which is the item's point and is well chosen. No wrong method reaches 6: the sign slip gives 10, reporting the x-sum gives -1, the root product gives -14. Worth recording that the item's own explanation misidentifies its strikeable option.

SM17A-A8.free_elimination: none found, and the set is well built against the residue attack that is natural here. Because x-2 divides p, write p(x) = (x-2)(2x^2 + cx + 6); then p(3) = 24 + 3c, so the answer must be divisible by 3. All four options (-42, 18, 30, 66) are multiples of 3, so that channel is closed. All four are also even, matching the forced parity of p(3) = 54 + 9a + 3b - 12 with a,b integers of the same parity -- again no strike. Sign: p(3) could be either sign a priori, so -42 is not strikeable.
SM17A-A8.note: Clean. Two conditions, a 2x2 system, then the remainder theorem -- four standard steps with no non-obvious insight, so I read it as medium rather than the labelled hard; it is long, not deep. Distractor '66' is the weakest of the three because it comes from a sign-reversed solution that satisfies neither given condition, so a solver who checks their a and b against p(2)=0 never produces it. No wrong method found that reaches 18.

SM17A-B1.free_elimination: TWO TO THREE STRUCK by a residue argument that costs one squaring. The vertex sits midway between the zeros, at half-distance 5/2, so the minimum is -a*(25/4) = -150, i.e. 25a = 600, which forces 4 | a. Of 6, 24, 25 and 60 only 24 is divisible by 4, so the constraint identifies the key uniquely without ever dividing 150 by 6.25. I score this 3 rather than 0 because the only thing it requires is the half-distance 5/2 -- the single idea the item exists to test -- and once a solver has that idea the divisibility read is faster and safer than the division. If the half-distance is not spotted, nothing is strikeable: all four options are positive, as the existence of a minimum requires, so the sign channel is dead.
SM17A-B1.note: Borderline. The distractor design is excellent -- 25 (min read as the y-intercept), 60 (distance not squared), 6 (full zero-to-zero distance squared) are the three real errors and each is named correctly. But the same non-integer intermediate 6.25 that makes the distractors work also makes the key the only option consistent with integrality, so a solver who gets the idea but fumbles the division is still funnelled to 24. Repair by choosing zeros an even distance apart, or a minimum value that does not force a mod-4 residue, so that at least two options survive the divisibility read.

SM17A-B2.free_elimination: none found, and the explanation's account of why is accurate and checks out. Every option minus 16 is a perfect square (9, 16, 25, 49), so the 'x-16 must come out square' filter strikes nothing; every option exceeds 21, so the bound x > 21 forced by x = 21 + 4*sqrt(x-16) strikes nothing; and the extraneous root x = 17 from u = -1 is correctly kept off the list, since it would have been freely strikeable by that same bound. Monotonicity does not help either: x - 4*sqrt(x-16) is increasing for x > 20 and all four options lie above 20, so the ordering of the options gives no information about which one hits 21.
SM17A-B2.note: Keep. The best-audited item in the batch -- the option-set note states the two cheap channels, and both claims verify. Cost: the item is fully backsolvable, since each option needs one square root and one subtraction (values come out 13, 16, 21, 37), so it measures substitution discipline rather than the u-substitution it is built around. That is acceptable at medium and is why I do not rate it hard. No wrong method reaches 41: the u = -1 branch gives 17, off-list.

SM17A-B3.free_elimination: THREE STRUCK. The 3/2 power means the base must be a perfect square for the result to be the printed integer 125 = 5^3. Subtracting 7 from each option -- the one operation the answer form invites anyway -- gives 5, 11, 18, 25, and only 25 is a square. That pins the key with no exponent work at all. The item's own OPTION-SET NOTE checks two other channels (the base must be positive and below 125, and no option makes x-7 = 125) and correctly reports that both are dead, but it does not check the squareness channel, which is the live one. Compare B2, where the author DID close exactly this channel by making all four offsets perfect squares -- the technique was known to the author and was not applied here.
SM17A-B3.note: DROP, or re-author the option set. Easy content is fine in the bank, but this is easy content whose answer is also free. The fix is the one B2 already demonstrates: offer offsets that are all perfect squares, e.g. keys of the form x-7 in {4, 9, 16, 25}, so the solver has to take 125^(2/3) rather than scan for a square. Note also that the three distractors (12, 18, 25) all have non-square offsets by construction, because each is a named arithmetic slip on 25 and 5; the tell is a side effect of the distractor brief, not an oversight in choosing numbers.

SM17A-B4.free_elimination: TWO STRUCK, by closure on divisibility. Integer growth per hour means P(3) = P(4)/b with b a positive integer, so the answer must divide 648. 216 and 72 do; 440 and 492 do not, and this is visible without arithmetic once one notices 440 and 492 are not even multiples of 3 while 648 is. That leaves 72 and 216, and the interpolation bound then does nothing to separate them since both lie between 24 and 648. Separately: 440 is exactly the linear-interpolation value and 492 the near-miss of it, so the two options that the divisibility argument kills are precisely the two a linear-thinking solver would choose -- the strike removes the wrong answers a weak solver wants, which is the benign direction, but it still halves the field for free.
SM17A-B4.note: Keep with reservations. The OPTION-SET NOTE is right that t=3 is off-centre so no geometric mean is offered, and right that sqrt(24*648) is not an integer -- both verified. But it audits the geometric-mean channel and misses the divisibility one. Structurally a near-twin of A3 (same b^3 = 27, same b = 3); if both ship into one form the second is nearly free once the first is solved. No wrong method reaches 216: 24*9 and 648/3 and the geometric mean of P(2) and P(4) are all valid routes to it.

SM17A-B5.free_elimination: TWO STRUCK, but only at a cost most solvers will not pay. For three positive reals with sum 12 and product 42, AM-GM on the pairwise products gives k >= 3*42^(2/3) = 36.2, which kills 27 and 29 and leaves 41 and 44. That needs a cube root, so I would not call it free; by the no-arithmetic standard the honest answer is n_struck = 0, and I record 2 because the bound is real and a strong solver may see it. One printed-number echo worth logging: the key 41 is exactly the printed constant 42 minus 1. That is a coincidence of the chosen triple, not a designed tell, but it is the kind of adjacency a guesser notices.
SM17A-B5.note: Keep. The uniqueness claim verifies exhaustively -- (2,3,7) is the only positive-integer triple with sum 12 and product 42. Distractor '27' (sums only two of the three pairwise products) is the sharpest in the batch. Two sloppinesses in the explanation, both harmless: it lists '1*1*42' and '1*42*1' as distinct factorisations and gives four sums for five listed triples, and it omits 1*1*42's sum of 44 from the mapping, which happens to collide with the distractor value 44 that is sourced elsewhere (2,4,6). No wrong method reaches 41.

SM17A-B6.free_elimination: none found. Options -41, -3, -2, 7 are four unrelated integers; no parity, sign or magnitude constraint applies to the output of a piecewise function, and the two branch formulas can produce values of either sign. The printed numbers 3, 5, 12, 8 do not echo any option in a way that separates them (-3 = 12 - 15 and 7 = 12 - 5 are both branch evaluations, i.e. distractors).
SM17A-B6.note: WRONG METHOD LANDS ON THE KEY -- flag. The inner input evaluates to exactly 1, and 1^2 = 1, so a solver who forgets to square computes 3(1) - 5 = -2 and gets the key. The quadratic rule is therefore inert: the item tests only the branch choice at the boundary, not the rule it selects. Worth fixing because the branch-boundary test is the item's real content and would be unharmed by moving the input off 1 -- but the boundary is what forces the input to be 1, so the repair means re-choosing the transformation and the breakpoint together (e.g. breakpoint at x <= 2 with 3x-8 evaluated at a larger x). Distractor '7' (the other branch at the boundary) is exactly right and is the one the item exists for.

SM17A-B7.free_elimination: ONE STRUCK, and a second is a recognisable trap rather than a strike. Evaluating f at any small integer -- f(2) = 23, f(3) = 23 -- bounds the minimum below 23 and kills 40.75; that is one multiplication, so near-free. 2.5 is transparently the vertex abscissa -b/(2a) = 20/8 and reads as the wrong-quantity trap, but calling it strikeable requires already knowing the vertex, so I do not count it. -3 survives the cheap read: ruling it out needs the discriminant 400 - 752 < 0, which is real arithmetic. Formatting: the two decimals (2.5, 40.75) are both distractors and the two integers (-3, 22) split key and distractor, so there is no typographic tell.
SM17A-B7.note: WRONG METHOD LANDS ON THE KEY -- flag, and it is a numeric coincidence specific to a = 4. The correct subtraction is b^2/(4a) = 400/16 = 25; a solver who instead subtracts (b/a)^2 = (-5)^2 = 25 gets the same number, because 4a = 16 = a^2 exactly when a = 4. So the 'factor out the leading coefficient and remember to multiply the squared half back by a' step -- the entire point of the item -- can be skipped and still score. The distractor 40.75 catches the solver who forgets the factor ENTIRELY, but not the one who applies it in the wrong place. Change the leading coefficient away from 4 and the coincidence disappears. Also the easiest item here despite the medium label.

SM17A-B8.free_elimination: none found. The two k values are 9 +/- 2*sqrt(22), irrational, so no option can be checked by substitution and backsolving is fully blocked -- a genuine strength. -7 is the product of the two k values and 18 the sum, both constants of the same k-quadratic, so an option-set reader cannot tell which relation is being asked without the stem. Parity, sign and magnitude all give nothing: -7, 2, 14, 18 span both signs and no constraint forces the sum positive a priori.
SM17A-B8.note: WRONG METHOD LANDS ON THE KEY -- flag, and this one is structural rather than coincidental. The answer is the sum of the roots of the discriminant quadratic, so it depends ONLY on the linear coefficient of (k-5)^2 - 8(k+4), namely -10 - 8 = -18. Every error confined to the constant term still returns 18: reading c as k instead of k+4, or as k-4, or dropping the +4 altogether, all give k^2 - 18k + (something) and sum 18. The stem's '+4' is therefore load-bearing for the setup and inert for the answer. Mitigating: the two distractors that matter, 14 (drops the factor a=2) and 2 (wrong sign on the whole 4ac term), both DO perturb the linear coefficient, so the item still discriminates the two errors most likely to occur. Genuinely the hardest item in the batch -- two nested layers plus the recognition that the k values need not be found -- and correctly labelled hard. Keep, with the caveat that it is less discriminating than its length suggests.
